topics.title: Introduction to the Java Collections Framework
topics.shortDescription: Understand the architecture of the Java Collections Framework, array limitations, Iterable and Collection hierarchy, and selection criteria.
learningObjectives: Explain the architecture and purpose of the Java Collections Framework (JCF)
Analyze the critical differences and trade-offs between static arrays and dynamic collections
Differentiate between the Collection interface hierarchy and the utility Collections class
Select optimal collection abstractions based on uniqueness, ordering, key-value lookup, and performance requirements
topics.conceptExplanation:
The Java Collections Framework (JCF) is a unified architecture for representing and manipulating collections of objects, independent of their implementation details. Prior to JDK 1.2, Java developers relied on primitive arrays, Vector, and Hashtable, which lacked a unified interface hierarchy and interoperability.

At the root of the collection hierarchy is the Iterable<T> interface, enabling the enhanced for-each loop and spliterators. Extending Iterable is Collection<T>, which defines core mutating and querying operations such as add(), remove(), contains(), size(), and stream(). The framework branches into three primary interfaces:
1. List<E>: An ordered sequence allowing positional access and duplicate elements (e.g., ArrayList, LinkedList).
2. Set<E>: A mathematical set disallowing duplicate elements (e.g., HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet).
3. Queue<E> and Deque<E>: Work queues enforcing specific processing orderings such as FIFO or LIFO (e.g., ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue).

Notice that Map<K,V> does NOT inherit from Collection<E> because it operates on key-value pairs rather than discrete elements. However, Map integrates seamlessly with the framework via view collections: keySet(), values(), and entrySet().

A fundamental distinction is between 'Collection' (the root interface) and 'Collections' (the utility class in java.util containing static algorithms like sort(), binarySearch(), unmodifiableList(), and synchronizedCollection()).

topics.title: ArrayList and LinkedList
topics.shortDescription: Deep dive into ArrayList and LinkedList internals, dynamic resizing mechanics, doubly-linked node traversal, time complexity, and selection benchmarks.
learningObjectives: Understand the internal backing array and growth policy of ArrayList
Analyze the doubly-linked Node<E> structure of Java's LinkedList
Compare time complexities: random access (O(1) vs O(N)) vs insertion/deletion at boundaries
Select the correct List implementation based on hardware cache locality and access patterns
topics.conceptExplanation:
Both ArrayList and LinkedList implement the List<E> interface, but their internal physical memory layouts lead to radically different performance trade-offs:

1. ArrayList Internals: Backed by a contiguous array Object[] elementData. When instantiated without parameters, default initial capacity is 10. When full, capacity increases by ~50% (newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)). Elements reside next to each other in physical RAM, leveraging CPU L1/L2 cache prefetching. Random access via get(index) is an instantaneous O(1) pointer arithmetic operation. However, inserting or deleting in the middle requires System.arraycopy to shift elements, costing O(N).

2. LinkedList Internals: Implemented as a Doubly-Linked List where each element is wrapped inside a heap-allocated Node object: class Node<E> { E item; Node<E> next; Node<E> prev; }. LinkedList also implements Deque<E>, allowing it to act as a stack or queue. Inserting or removing at head or tail is strictly O(1) reference reassignment with zero array copying. However, random access via get(index) requires traversing nodes from whichever end is closer (index < size/2), taking O(N) time.

3. Cache Locality Reality: In modern computer architectures, ArrayList almost always outperforms LinkedList even for frequent middle insertions unless list sizes are colossal, because LinkedList nodes are scattered across the JVM heap, causing frequent CPU cache misses and 24-byte per-node memory overhead.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     ARRAYLIST VS LINKEDLIST MEMORY LAYOUT               |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ARRAYLIST (Contiguous Heap Array):                                      |
|   Index:     [0]       [1]       [2]       [3]       [4] (Capacity 10)  |
|   Element: ["Alice"] ["Bob"] ["Charlie"] ["Diana"] [null] ...            |
|   * get(i): O(1) via baseAddress + i * 8. Cache-friendly prefetching.   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| LINKEDLIST (Scattered Node Pointers):                                   |
|   [Head] -> [prev|Alice|next] <-> [prev|Bob|next] <-> [prev|Charlie|next]|
|   * get(i): O(N) sequential pointer traversal. Cache miss penalty.       |
|   * addFirst()/addLast(): O(1) constant pointer updates.                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.title: Vector and Stack
topics.shortDescription: Explore legacy synchronized collections: Vector and Stack, the LIFO principle, underflow conditions, and modern alternatives like ArrayDeque.
learningObjectives: Examine legacy Vector synchronization mechanics and compare with modern ArrayList
Understand the classic java.util.Stack class and its LIFO (Last-In First-Out) operations

Evaluate why java.util.Stack is considered legacy and adopt ArrayDeque as the modern replacement
topics.conceptExplanation:
Vector and Stack are legacy classes originating from JDK 1.0, retrofitted in JDK 1.2 into the Collections Framework.

1. Vector Internals: Like ArrayList, Vector is backed by an array Object[] elementData. However, almost every method in Vector (add, remove, get, size) is declared with the 'synchronized' keyword. This introduces intrinsic lock acquisition overhead on every operation even in single-threaded environments. Furthermore, Vector doubles its capacity by default (100% growth) when full, unlike ArrayList's 50% expansion.

2. Stack Internals: java.util.Stack extends Vector. This design violates modern object-oriented principles because inheritance implies 'is-a', yet a Stack is conceptually not a general-purpose indexed array. Because it inherits from Vector, clients can call stack.insertElementAt(item, 0) or stack.remove(2), completely violating the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) contract.

3. LIFO Operations: Stack provides push(item), pop() (removes & returns top, throws EmptyStackException if empty), peek() (looks at top without removing), and empty().

4. Modern Replacement (ArrayDeque): For single-threaded stacks, official Java documentation recommends Deque<E> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(). ArrayDeque is faster, does not synchronize unnecessarily, has no node allocation overhead, and strictly preserves LIFO semantics.

topics.moduleTitle: SECTION A: Java Collections Framework
topics.title: HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet
topics.shortDescription: Master the Set interface: element uniqueness, hash bucket mechanics in HashSet, insertion ordering in LinkedHashSet, and Red-Black tree sorting in TreeSet.
learningObjectives: Understand the Set interface contract prohibiting duplicate elements
Explain how HashSet is backed by a HashMap and relies on equals() and hashCode()
Analyze the doubly-linked bucket mechanism of LinkedHashSet maintaining insertion order
Explore TreeSet's Red-Black Tree architecture, O(log N) operations, and natural vs Comparator ordering
topics.conceptExplanation:
The Set<E> interface models a mathematical set containing no duplicate elements (at most one null in hash-based implementations). Java offers three primary general-purpose Set implementations:

1. HashSet: Backed internally by a HashMap where set elements serve as map keys, and a dummy Object (PRESENT) serves as the value. Elements are distributed across hash buckets using their hashCode(). Offers constant time O(1) performance for add(), remove(), and contains(), assuming a good hash function. Iteration order is completely arbitrary and can change upon resizing.

2. LinkedHashSet: Extends HashSet, but each entry is also wired into a doubly-linked list that traces insertion order. When iterating, elements are yielded in the exact sequence they were added. Performance remains near O(1) with slight overhead for link maintenance.

3. TreeSet: Implements NavigableSet and is backed by a Red-Black Tree (TreeMap). Elements are maintained in strictly sorted order. Elements must implement Comparable<E> or a custom Comparator<E> must be supplied at construction. Time complexity for add, remove, and contains is guaranteed O(log N). TreeSet rejects null elements if using natural ordering because null cannot be compared.

Crucial Contract: In HashSet and LinkedHashSet, two objects e1 and e2 are duplicates if e1.equals(e2). In TreeSet, uniqueness is determined exclusively by comparator.compare(e1, e2) == 0 (or e1.compareTo(e2) == 0), NOT equals()!

All three Set instances reject duplicate additions when element already exists.

topics.conceptExplanation:
HashMap<K, V> is Java's most widely used key-value data structure, offering average O(1) time complexity for put() and get().

1. Internal Architecture: Backed by a Node<K, V>[] table array. The default initial capacity is 16 and default load factor is 0.75. When entries reach 16 * 0.75 = 12, the table doubles (rehashing). The bucket index is computed as: index = (n - 1) & hash(key), where hash(key) uses a bitwise spread function: (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16) to minimize collisions.

2. Collision Handling & Treeification (Java 8+): In JDK 7, collisions were resolved exclusively via singly-linked lists (separate chaining), vulnerable to denial-of-service degradation to O(N). In JDK 8+, when a single bucket exceeds TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8 entries) and table capacity is at least 64 (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY), the linked list converts into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeNode), reducing worst-case lookup to O(log N). If bucket size falls to 6 (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a list.

3. The equals() and hashCode() Contract: If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() MUST equal b.hashCode(). If violated, HashMap searches the wrong bucket and fails to locate existing keys. Keys must be immutable: mutating a key after insertion changes its hashCode(), stranding the entry permanently.

4. LinkedHashMap: Extends HashMap by overlaying a doubly-linked list over all entries. It can maintain insertion order (default) or access order (useful for Least Recently Used (LRU) caches by overriding removeEldestEntry()).

| [Bucket 1] -> [KeyA: Val1] -> [KeyB: Val2] -> null  (Separate Chaining)  |

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| LINKEDHASHMAP (Access-Order LRU Mode):                                  |
|   Head <-> [Oldest Accessed] <-> [Recent] <-> [Most Recent] <-> Tail    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.conceptExplanation:
TreeMap and Hashtable represent contrasting specialized map implementations in Java:

1. TreeMap Architecture: TreeMap implements NavigableMap<K, V> (which extends SortedMap<K, V>). It is backed by a self-balancing Red-Black Tree. Keys are ordered according to their natural ordering (implementing Comparable<K>) or by a Comparator<K> provided at construction. All fundamental operations (get, put, remove, containsKey) run in guaranteed O(log N) time.

2. NavigableMap Capabilities: TreeMap allows rich range and closest-match queries: firstKey(), lastKey(), floorKey(k) (largest key <= k), ceilingKey(k) (smallest key >= k), lowerKey(k), higherKey(k), and range views like subMap(fromKey, toKey).

3. Hashtable (Legacy): Originating from JDK 1.0, Hashtable is a synchronized hash table. Like Vector, its methods are synchronized, leading to heavy lock contention. It does NOT permit null keys or null values (throws NullPointerException immediately). In modern concurrent software, Hashtable is obsolete and replaced by ConcurrentHashMap.

4. Null Policy Summary: HashMap permits one null key and multiple null values. TreeMap permits no null keys (throws NPE on compareTo) but permits null values. Hashtable forbids both null keys and null values.

learningObjectives: Differentiate Queue method contracts: throwing exceptions (add, remove, element) vs returning special values (offer, poll, peek)

topics.conceptExplanation:
The Queue<E> and Deque<E> interfaces represent collections designed for holding elements prior to processing.

1. Queue Method Pairs: Queue provides two sets of methods for common operations:
- Insert: add(e) throws IllegalStateException if capacity exceeded; offer(e) returns false.
- Remove: remove() throws NoSuchElementException if empty; poll() returns null.
- Examine: element() throws NoSuchElementException if empty; peek() returns null.
In production, the non-throwing forms (offer, poll, peek) are strongly preferred.

2. Deque (Double-Ended Queue): Deque extends Queue, allowing elements to be inserted and extracted from both head and tail. ArrayDeque is backed by a circular array (ring buffer) with head and tail pointers. It has no node overhead (unlike LinkedList) and does not synchronize (unlike Stack). It is the recommended implementation for both LIFO stacks and FIFO queues.

3. PriorityQueue Architecture: PriorityQueue implements Queue but does NOT enforce FIFO order. Instead, elements are ordered according to their natural ordering or a custom Comparator. Internally, it is backed by an array representing a complete Binary Min-Heap:
- Root at index 0 holds the minimum element.
- For node at index i: Left child = 2i + 1, Right child = 2i + 2, Parent = (i - 1) / 2.
- Insertion (offer) appends to the end and 'percolates up' in O(log N) time.
- Extraction (poll) removes the root, moves the last element to the top, and 'percolates down' in O(log N) time.
- Peek is instantaneous O(1) by accessing index 0 directly.

topics.shortDescription: Master safe collection iteration: Iterator, ListIterator bidirectional traversal, fail-fast mechanics, ConcurrentModificationException, and Comparable vs Comparator sorting.
learningObjectives: Traverse collections safely using Iterator and understand why collection.remove() throws ConcurrentModificationException during for-each loops

topics.conceptExplanation:
Iterating and ordering collections safely are cornerstones of robust Java software.

1. The Iterator<E> Interface: Iterable<T> defines iterator(). An Iterator provides hasNext(), next(), and remove(). Crucially, iterator.remove() is the ONLY safe way to remove elements while traversing a standard collection. If code modifies the collection directly (e.g., list.remove()) during an enhanced for-each loop, the iterator detects an unexpected change in internal modCount and immediately throws ConcurrentModificationException. This is known as the fail-fast principle.

2. ListIterator<E>: A specialized subinterface for List collections providing bidirectional traversal:
- Forward: hasNext(), next(), nextIndex()
- Backward: hasPrevious(), previous(), previousIndex()
- In-Place Mutation: set(e) replaces the last visited element; add(e) inserts an element at current position.

3. Comparable<T> (Natural Ordering): Implemented directly inside a domain class (e.g., class Employee implements Comparable<Employee>). It requires defining int compareTo(T o):
- Negative: this < o
- Zero: this == o (should be consistent with equals())
- Positive: this > o

4. Comparator<T> (Custom External Ordering): A standalone functional interface @FunctionalInterface int compare(T o1, T o2). It allows multiple arbitrary sorting strategies without modifying the domain class (e.g., sort by salary, sort by hire date, reverse sort).

topics.conceptExplanation:
Generics, introduced in Java 5, provide compile-time type safety by allowing classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on parameterized types.

1. Motivation: In Java 1.4 and earlier, collections stored raw Objects. Extracting an element required explicit casting: String s = (String) list.get(0);. If an incorrect object slipped in, the code compiled cleanly but crashed at runtime with ClassCastException. Generics detect type mismatches during compilation, catching bugs before production.

2. Generic Classes & Interfaces: A class can define one or more formal type parameters: public class Box<T> { private T value; }. Standard conventions use: T (Type), E (Element), K (Key), V (Value), N (Number).

3. Bounded Type Parameters: To restrict types to a specific hierarchy, use bounded type parameters: <T extends Number>. This guarantees that T is either Number or a subclass of Number (e.g., Integer, Double), enabling methods like doubleValue() to be called inside.

4. JVM Type Erasure: Java implements generics using type erasure to ensure backward compatibility with pre-Java 5 bytecode. At compile time, the Java compiler verifies type correctness, replaces type parameters with their bounds (or Object if unbounded), and inserts necessary casts. At runtime, the JVM has no knowledge of type parameters (e.g., List<String> and List<Integer> share the same compiled Class object: List.class). Consequently, you cannot do: new T(), instanceof T, or create generic arrays new T[10].

topics.moduleTitle: SECTION B: Generics and Functional Programming
topics.title: Wildcards and Advanced Generics
topics.shortDescription: Master generic variance: unbounded wildcards (<?>), upper-bounded (<? extends T>), lower-bounded (<? super T>), and the essential PECS principle.
learningObjectives: Understand why generic types are invariant (List<Integer> is NOT a List<Number>)
Master Upper-Bounded Wildcards (<? extends T>) for read-only producer collections

topics.conceptExplanation:
One of the most confusing aspects of Java generics is variance: although Integer is a subclass of Number, List<Integer> is NOT a subtype of List<Number>. If it were, you could do: List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>(); nums.add(3.14);, which corrupts the underlying Integer list. In Java terminology, generic types are invariant.

To write flexible generic methods that accept related collections, Java introduces Wildcards (?):

1. Unbounded Wildcard (<?>): Represents any unknown type. Useful for operations that only rely on Object methods or collection structure (e.g., list.size(), list.clear()). You cannot add anything to List<?> except null.

2. Upper-Bounded Wildcard (<? extends T>): Accepts T or any subclass of T (covariance). This makes the collection a PRODUCER: you can safely read elements from it as type T, but you CANNOT write elements into it (except null) because the compiler cannot know which specific subtype the list actually holds.

3. Lower-Bounded Wildcard (<? super T>): Accepts T or any superclass of T (contravariance). This makes the collection a CONSUMER: you can safely write instances of T into it. However, reading from it only yields raw Object references.

4. The PECS Principle: 'Producer Extends, Consumer Super'.
- If your method parameter produces data for your method to read, use <? extends T>.
- If your method parameter consumes data that your method writes into it, use <? super T>.
- If you both read and write, use an exact type parameter <T> without wildcards.

|   Number n = src.get(0); // OK: Every item is guaranteed to be a Number  |
|   src.add(10);           // COMPILER ERROR! Cannot write to producer     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| CONSUMER SUPER (<? super Integer>):                                     |
|   List<? super Integer> dest = new ArrayList<Number>();                 |
|   dest.add(42);          // OK: Integer is guaranteed safe to write      |
|   Integer x = dest.get(0);// COMPILER ERROR! Reading only yields Object |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)           |
|                     ^ Consumer                ^ Producer                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.shortDescription: Adopt functional programming in Java: lambda syntax, parameters, single-expression vs block lambdas, effectively final variable capture, and invokedynamic mechanics.
learningObjectives: Transition from verbose anonymous inner classes to concise lambda expressions

topics.conceptExplanation:
Introduced in Java 8, lambda expressions brought functional programming paradigms to Java, enabling behavior to be passed as data without verbose anonymous inner classes.

1. Syntax Structure: A lambda expression consists of three parts:
   (parameters) -> expression   OR   (parameters) -> { statements; }
- Parameter types can usually be inferred by the compiler: (a, b) -> a + b.
- A single parameter does not require parentheses: x -> x * x.
- Zero parameters require empty parentheses: () -> System.out.println('Hello').

2. Single-Expression vs Block Lambdas: If the body contains a single expression, curly braces and the 'return' keyword are omitted. If the body contains multiple statements or local declarations, curly braces and explicit return statements are required.

3. Variable Capture (Effectively Final): Lambdas can capture instance variables, static variables, and local variables from their enclosing scope. However, any local variable accessed inside a lambda must be final or effectively final (i.e., its value is never mutated after initialization). This restriction prevents concurrency race conditions between the stack frame where the variable was created and the lambda execution context.

4. Lambdas vs Anonymous Inner Classes: While anonymous classes create a new .class file on disk and maintain an independent 'this' reference, lambdas are translated using the invokedynamic (indy) bytecode instruction and LambdaMetafactory. They do not generate extra class files and 'this' refers to the enclosing instance.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.conceptExplanation:
A functional interface is an interface that declares exactly one abstract method (Single Abstract Method or SAM). It may declare any number of default or static methods, as well as abstract methods matching public methods of java.lang.Object.

The @FunctionalInterface annotation informs the compiler to verify SAM compliance. Java 8 introduced java.util.function with four foundational functional interfaces:

1. Predicate<T>: Represents a boolean-valued condition: boolean test(T t). Used for filtering and validation. Supports composition: p1.and(p2), p1.or(p2), p1.negate().

2. Function<T, R>: Represents a transformation from an input of type T to a result of type R: R apply(T t). Used in mapping operations. Supports function chaining: f1.andThen(f2) (executes f1 then f2) and f1.compose(f2) (executes f2 then f1).

3. Consumer<T>: Accepts a single input argument and returns no result (void): void accept(T t). Used for side effects, such as printing, saving to database, or dispatching events. Supports chaining via andThen().

4. Supplier<T>: Takes no arguments and produces a result of type T: T get(). Used for factory generation and lazy evaluation.

Bi-Variants & Primitives: BiPredicate<T, U>, BiFunction<T, U, R>, BiConsumer<T, U> accept two inputs. Primitive specializations (e.g., IntPredicate, LongConsumer, ToDoubleFunction<T>) avoid autoboxing performance penalties.

topics.conceptExplanation:
Method references, introduced in Java 8, provide a compact, easy-to-read syntax for lambda expressions that do nothing more than call an existing named method. The double colon (::) separates the class or object name from the method name.

There are four distinct categories of method references:

1. Reference to a Static Method (ContainingClass::staticMethodName):
   Lambda: (s) -> Integer.parseInt(s)
   Method Ref: Integer::parseInt

2. Reference to an Instance Method of a Particular Existing Object (containingObject::instanceMethodName) - Bound Instance:
   Lambda: (msg) -> System.out.println(msg)
   Method Ref: System.out::println

3. Reference to an Instance Method of an Arbitrary Object of a Particular Type (ContainingType::methodName) - Unbound Instance:
   Lambda: (s) -> s.toUpperCase()   OR   (s1, s2) -> s1.compareToIgnoreCase(s2)
   Method Ref: String::toUpperCase  OR   String::compareToIgnoreCase
   Here, the first argument becomes the target (invoking object) of the method call.

4. Reference to a Constructor (ClassName::new):
   Lambda: () -> new ArrayList<>()   OR   (size) -> new int[size]
   Method Ref: ArrayList::new        OR   int[]::new

Readability Principle: If a lambda expression simply delegates to a method without introducing complex logic or modifying arguments, replace it with a method reference.

The Stream API (java.util.stream), introduced in Java 8, transforms how collections are manipulated by moving from imperative 'how to do it' loops to declarative 'what to do' functional pipelines.

1. Collection vs Stream:
- A Collection is an in-memory data structure that holds elements. Every element is computed before it can be added.
- A Stream is a conceptual view over a data sequence. A stream does not store data; it conveys elements from a source (collection, array, I/O channel) through a pipeline of computational steps.

2. Anatomy of a Stream Pipeline: A stream pipeline consists of three distinct phases:
   Source -> Intermediate Operation(s) -> Terminal Operation

3. Intermediate Operations (Lazy): Methods such as filter(Predicate), map(Function), sorted(), distinct(), limit(long), skip(long). They are lazy: no computation occurs when an intermediate operation is called. They simply record the operation on the pipeline.

4. Terminal Operations (Eager): Methods such as collect(Collector), forEach(Consumer), count(), reduce(), min(), max(). A terminal operation triggers the actual execution of the pipeline, pulling elements from the source, passing them through the fused intermediate operations, and producing a concrete result or side-effect.

5. Single-Use Lifecycle: Once a terminal operation has been executed on a Stream, the stream is considered consumed and closed. Attempting to reuse a closed stream throws IllegalStateException: 'stream has already been operated upon or closed'.

    .filter(s -> s.getGpa() >= 3.8)      // Intermediate (Lazy)
    .map(Student::getName)               // Intermediate (Lazy)
    .sorted()                            // Intermediate (Lazy)
    .limit(5)                            // Intermediate (Lazy)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());       // Terminal (Executes Pipeline)

topics.conceptExplanation:
Advanced Stream operations enable multi-dimensional aggregation, restructuring, and statistical analytics.

1. Reductions (reduce): A reduction combines elements into a single summary result using an associative accumulator function. Java offers: Optional<T> reduce(BinaryOperator<T> accumulator) and T reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T> accumulator). For example: numbers.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum).

2. Flattening Hierarchies (flatMap): When elements of a stream are themselves collections (e.g., Stream<List<String>>), standard map() would produce a nested Stream<Stream<String>>. flatMap(Collection::stream) flattens nested streams into a single Stream<String>.

3. Grouping (Collectors.groupingBy): Equivalent to SQL 'GROUP BY'. It partitions elements into a Map<K, List<T>> based on a classifier function: employees.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment)).

4. Downstream Collectors: groupingBy can take a secondary collector to aggregate grouped items into counts, averages, or transformed sets: groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::getSalary)).

5. Partitioning (Collectors.partitioningBy): A specialized two-way grouping based on a Predicate, returning Map<Boolean, List<T>> with keys true and false.

topics.conceptExplanation:
NullPointerException (NPE) is historically one of the most common runtime bugs in Java. To combat this, Java 8 introduced java.util.Optional<T>, a single-value container that either wraps a non-null reference or is empty.

1. Creation Methods:
- Optional.of(value): Wraps a non-null value. Throws NullPointerException immediately if value is null.
- Optional.ofNullable(value): Safely wraps a value. If value is null, returns Optional.empty().
- Optional.empty(): Returns an empty Optional instance.

2. Accessing & Unwrapping:
- isPresent() / isEmpty() (Java 11+): Queries presence state.
- ifPresent(Consumer): Executes action only if value exists.
- get(): Extracts value; throws NoSuchElementException if empty. Avoid calling get() without isPresent()!

3. Fallback Strategies:
- orElse(defaultVal): Returns value or defaultVal. Note: defaultVal expression is ALWAYS evaluated eagerly!
- orElseGet(Supplier): Lazily invokes supplier only when Optional is empty. Crucial for expensive fallback calculations.
- orElseThrow(Supplier): Throws a custom exception if empty: opt.orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException()).

4. Functional Transformations:
- map(Function): Transforms inner value; returns empty Optional if source is empty or function returns null.
- flatMap(Function): Prevents nested Optional<Optional<T>> when mapping function itself returns an Optional.
- filter(Predicate): Keeps value if predicate matches; returns empty otherwise.

5. Design Best Practices: Optional is designed strictly as a METHOD RETURN TYPE for methods that might not return a value. Never use Optional as a class field (it is not Serializable), method parameter, or inside collections (e.g., Map<K, Optional<V>>).

topics.conceptExplanation:
Enterprise Java applications require predictable, informative error handling mechanisms.

1. The Throwable Hierarchy:
- java.lang.Error: Fatal system-level failures (e.g., OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) that applications should not catch.
- java.lang.Exception (Checked): Recoverable business conditions (e.g., IOException, SQLException). The compiler enforces handling via try-catch or method declaration (throws).
- java.lang.RuntimeException (Unchecked): Programming errors and state violations (e.g., NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException). Handled selectively; compiler does not force throws declarations.

2. Custom Exception Architecture: Build domain-specific exceptions by extending Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked). Always provide constructors accepting (String message) and (String message, Throwable cause).

3. Exception Chaining: When catching a lower-level exception (e.g., SQLException) in a data layer and translating it to a domain exception (e.g., AccountNotFoundException), pass the original exception as the 'cause'. This preserves the original stack trace for debugging.

4. Multi-Catch (Java 7+): Handles multiple unrelated exceptions in a single block: catch (IOException | SQLException e). In a multi-catch, parameter 'e' is implicitly final.

5. Finally Semantics: Code in finally executes regardless of whether an exception was thrown, caught, or unhandled. Never place a 'return' or 'throw' statement inside a finally block, as it swallows any in-flight exception being propagated.

topics.conceptExplanation:
Handling file systems and OS resources safely requires strict cleanup guarantees to prevent file handle and socket leaks.

1. Legacy java.io vs Modern java.nio.file (NIO.2):
- java.io.File lacked rich metadata, failed silently (returning boolean false instead of throwing informative exceptions), and did not handle symbolic links well.
- java.nio.file (introduced in Java 7) introduces Path (object-oriented file locator) and the static Files utility class (Files.readString, Files.writeString, Files.lines, Files.copy, Files.delete). NIO.2 throws informative, granular exceptions.

2. Stream Processing:
- Byte Streams: InputStream / OutputStream (operate on raw 8-bit bytes, ideal for binary data like images or PDFs).
- Character Streams: Reader / Writer (operate on 16-bit characters, handling character encodings like UTF-8).
- Buffering: BufferedReader and BufferedWriter buffer chunks into memory, avoiding costly disk I/O on every single character read.

3. Try-with-Resources (ARM): Prior to Java 7, closing resources in finally required nested try-catch blocks. Try-with-resources automatically invokes close() on any resource implementing java.lang.AutoCloseable at the end of the statement, even if an exception occurs.

4. Suppressed Exceptions: If both the try block and the auto-generated close() method throw exceptions, the try-block exception is thrown as primary, while the close() exception is attached as a suppressed exception (retrievable via e.getSuppressed()).

|     // Process content                                                  |
| } // <-- JVM automatically calls reader.close() here!                   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| SUPPRESSED EXCEPTIONS HANDLING:                                         |
|   1. Try Block throws: FileCorruptedException (Primary)                 |
|   2. reader.close() throws: IOException (Suppressed)                    |
|   -> Catch receives FileCorruptedException                              |

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.shortDescription: Inspect and manipulate metadata dynamically: custom annotations (@Retention, @Target), the Java Reflection API (Class, Method, Field), and runtime validation engines.

topics.conceptExplanation:
Annotations and Reflection allow Java programs to inspect and modify their own structure dynamically, forming the backbone of frameworks like Spring Boot, Hibernate, and JUnit.

1. Annotations: Metadata tags placed on classes, methods, fields, or parameters that do not alter program execution directly. Meta-annotations configure their lifecycle:
- @Retention: Defines how long the annotation is retained. SOURCE (discarded by compiler), CLASS (retained in .class file, ignored by JVM), or RUNTIME (retained in VM, inspectable via reflection).
- @Target: Specifies where the annotation can be applied (ElementType.TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER).

2. Java Reflection API: Located in java.lang.reflect, it provides runtime access to the internal representation of types:
- Class<?> clazz = obj.getClass();
- Field[] fields = clazz.getDeclaredFields();
- Method[] methods = clazz.getDeclaredMethods();
- field.setAccessible(true): Bypasses private encapsulation checks (subject to JVM module system boundaries).
- method.invoke(instance, args...): Invokes a method dynamically at runtime.

3. Trade-offs & Limitations: Reflection incurs performance overhead because method calls bypass JIT compiler optimizations. It breaks compile-time type safety and can violate internal encapsulation. Use reflection for reusable framework utilities and dependency injection, not everyday application logic.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.conceptExplanation:
Modern Java (Java 14 - 17+) introduced powerful language features that eliminate boilerplate and enforce strict type hierarchies.

1. Advanced Enums: In Java, an enum is a full-fledged class. Enums can maintain fields, constructors (implicitly private), and methods. They can even declare abstract methods that every enum constant must individually implement (Constant-Specific Method). Java provides high-performance bit-vector collections: EnumSet and array-indexed EnumMap.

2. Java Records (JDK 16+): Records provide a concise syntax for declaring immutable data carriers. When you write:
   record Person(String name, int age) {}
the compiler automatically synthesizes: private final fields, a canonical constructor, component getter methods (name(), age()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Compact constructors allow validation without repeating assignments: public Person { Objects.requireNonNull(name); }.

3. Sealed Classes and Interfaces (JDK 17+): Traditionally, a class was either open to any extension or closed via 'final'. Sealed classes allow a class or interface to restrict exactly which subclasses are permitted to extend or implement it:
   public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
Every permitted subclass must be declared as final, sealed, or non-sealed.

4. Exhaustive Pattern Matching: When switching over a sealed hierarchy, the compiler knows all possible subclasses, enabling exhaustive pattern matching without needing a defensive 'default' clause.

topics.shortDescription: Master concurrent execution: Process vs Thread, Thread lifecycle states, Thread class vs Runnable interface, start() vs run(), sleep(), join(), and daemon threads.

topics.conceptExplanation:
Multithreading allows a Java program to perform multiple concurrent tasks, taking full advantage of modern multi-core CPUs.

1. Process vs Thread:
- A Process is an executing application with an isolated address space allocated by the operating system.
- A Thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. All threads in a JVM process share the Heap and Metaspace, but each thread maintains its own private Call Stack and Program Counter (PC) register.

2. Thread States (Thread.State enum):
- NEW: Thread created but not yet started.
- RUNNABLE: Executing or ready to execute on the CPU.
- BLOCKED: Waiting to acquire a monitor lock to enter a synchronized block/method.
- WAITING: Waiting indefinitely for another thread (e.g., Object.wait(), Thread.join()).
- TIMED_WAITING: Waiting for a specified time period (e.g., Thread.sleep(millis), join(millis)).
- TERMINATED: Run method has completed execution or thrown an unhandled exception.

3. Creating Threads: Extending Thread vs Implementing Runnable:
- Extending Thread binds the task to a single class hierarchy (Java does not support multiple inheritance).
- Implementing Runnable (a functional interface with void run()) separates the task to be executed from the thread runner mechanism, enabling reuse and compatibility with thread pools.

4. Crucial Trap: start() vs run():
- Calling thread.start() asks the JVM and OS to spawn a new native thread and invoke run() asynchronously on that new stack.
- Calling thread.run() directly merely executes the method synchronously on the CURRENT caller thread with zero multithreading!

5. Coordination & Daemons:
- Thread.sleep(ms): Temporarily suspends the current thread without releasing acquired locks.
- thread.join(): Blocks the calling thread until the target thread finishes execution.
- setDaemon(true): Marks a thread as a background service thread (e.g., garbage collector). The JVM terminates immediately when all user (non-daemon) threads complete, killing any remaining daemon threads abruptly.

topics.title: Synchronization and Thread Safety
topics.shortDescription: Prevent race conditions and memory corruption: synchronized methods and blocks, intrinsic monitor locks, the volatile keyword, Atomic variables (CAS), and deadlocks.
learningObjectives: Identify race conditions caused by non-atomic compound operations (e.g., count++) on shared mutable state
Apply synchronized methods and synchronized blocks using intrinsic object monitors
Understand the volatile keyword: visibility guarantees, happens-before relationship, and instruction reordering
Utilize lock-free Atomic variables (AtomicInteger, AtomicReference) using hardware Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
topics.conceptExplanation:
When multiple threads read and write shared mutable state without proper coordination, race conditions occur, producing corrupt data and unpredictable bugs.

1. Race Conditions & Atomicity: Consider count++. In bytecode, count++ is THREE separate operations:
   (1) Read count from memory into register, (2) Increment register value, (3) Write register back to memory.
If two threads execute this simultaneously, their reads and writes interleave, causing lost updates.

2. Intrinsic Locks (Synchronized): Every object in Java has an associated monitor lock:
- synchronized void method(): Acquires the lock on 'this' (or the Class object for static methods) before executing.
- synchronized(lockObj) { ... }: Protects a specific critical section. Prefer private final Object lock = new Object(); to prevent external code from acquiring your internal lock.

3. The volatile Keyword: Modern CPUs cache values in per-core L1/L2 caches. If thread A writes to a variable, thread B on another core might not see the new value due to cache staleness. Declaring a variable 'volatile' guarantees visibility:
- Writes to a volatile variable are immediately flushed to main memory.
- Reads are always fetched directly from main memory.
- Prevents instruction reordering around the read/write (happens-before guarantee).
- NOTE: volatile guarantees VISIBILITY, but NOT ATOMICITY for compound operations like count++.

4. Lock-Free Atomic Variables (java.util.concurrent.atomic): Classes like AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, and AtomicReference utilize CPU-level hardware atomic instructions (Compare-And-Swap or CAS). They deliver thread safety without lock acquisition overhead.

5. Deadlocks: Occurs when Thread 1 holds Lock A and waits for Lock B, while Thread 2 holds Lock B and waits for Lock A. Prevent deadlocks by always acquiring multiple locks in a globally consistent, uniform order.
topics.visualDiagram:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     RACE CONDITION VS SYNCHRONIZATION                   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| RACE CONDITION (count = 0, both threads do count++):                    |
|   Thread A: Reads count (0) -> Computes 0+1                             |
|   Thread B: Reads count (0) -> Computes 0+1 -> Writes 1 to count        |
|   Thread A: Writes 1 to count   (LOST UPDATE! Expected 2, Got 1)        |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| INTRINSIC MONITOR LOCK:                                                 |
|   Thread A acquires Lock -> Enters Critical Section -> Writes 1 -> Exit |
|   Thread B is BLOCKED until Thread A exits -> Reads 1 -> Writes 2       |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| COMPARE-AND-SWAP (CAS) in AtomicInteger:                                |
|   Atomic update: if (current == expected) current = newValue;           |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

topics.moduleTitle: SECTION D: Multithreading and Concurrency
topics.title: ExecutorService and Thread Pools
topics.shortDescription: Scale concurrent workloads: why raw threads are expensive, Executors factory pools, Callable vs Runnable, Future result contracts, and graceful shutdown.
learningObjectives: Explain the operating system overhead of unbounded new Thread() instantiation (memory and context switching)
Master the ExecutorService lifecycle and thread pool architectures (Fixed, Cached, Single, Scheduled)
Differentiate Runnable (void return, no checked exceptions) from Callable<V> (returns V, throws Exception)
Manage asynchronous task results with Future<V> and execute graceful pool shutdowns
topics.conceptExplanation:
Creating a native thread in Java incurs significant overhead: allocating 1MB of stack space in RAM, kernel context switching, and OS scheduling. In high-throughput servers, spawning 'new Thread()' per request can crash the JVM with OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread. The Executor framework (java.util.concurrent) solves this by decoupling task submission from thread execution through thread pooling.

1. Thread Pool Mechanics: A thread pool maintains a fixed or dynamic pool of pre-allocated worker threads that pull submitted tasks from an internal BlockingQueue. When a task completes, the worker thread remains alive to execute the next task, amortizing creation overhead to zero.

2. Executors Factory Methods:
- Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n): Fixed number of threads with an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Best for predictable, bounded workloads.
- Executors.newCachedThreadPool(): Dynamically creates threads as needed (60s idle timeout) using SynchronousQueue. Best for short-lived bursts.
- Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(): Single worker ensuring strictly sequential execution.
- Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n): Supports scheduled delayed execution and recurring intervals.

3. Runnable vs Callable<V>:
- Runnable: void run(), cannot return a value or throw checked exceptions.
- Callable<V>: V call() throws Exception, returns a computed result and can propagate exceptions.

4. The Future<V> Interface: Submitting a task via executor.submit() immediately returns a Future<V> token representing the pending result:
- future.get(): Blocks until the task completes and returns result V (or throws ExecutionException if task failed).
- future.get(timeout, unit): Timed blocking.
- future.isDone(), future.cancel(true).

5. Graceful Shutdown: Thread pools must be explicitly shut down, or their non-daemon worker threads will prevent the JVM from exiting:
   executor.shutdown(); // Rejects new tasks, completes queued tasks
   executor.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

topics.shortDescription: Write non-blocking reactive pipelines: CompletableFuture, supplyAsync, transformations (thenApply, thenAccept), composition (thenCompose, thenCombine), and error handling.
learningObjectives: Recognize the limitations of traditional Future<T> (blocking get() call, no callback chaining)

topics.conceptExplanation:
Traditional Future<V> introduced in Java 5 had severe limitations: calling future.get() blocked the calling thread, and there was no way to chain callbacks, combine multiple futures, or handle exceptions asynchronously. Java 8 introduced CompletableFuture<T>, implementing both Future<T> and CompletionStage<T> to enable reactive, non-blocking asynchronous programming.

1. Task Creation:
- CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier<U>): Runs task asynchronously on ForkJoinPool.commonPool() and returns result.
- CompletableFuture.runAsync(Runnable): Runs a void task asynchronously.

2. Transformation & Chaining (Callbacks):
- thenApply(Function<T, U>): Transforms result asynchronously when ready (like Stream map).
- thenAccept(Consumer<T>): Consumes result with side-effect (void return).
- thenRun(Runnable): Runs an action after completion without inspecting result.

3. Combining & Composing:
- thenCompose(Function<T, CompletableFuture<U>>): Chains two dependent futures where the second future relies on the output of the first (flatMap).
- thenCombine(CompletableFuture<U>, BiFunction<T, U, V>): Runs two independent futures in parallel and merges their results.
- CompletableFuture.allOf(futures...): Waits for an arbitrary batch of futures to complete.

4. Exception Handling:
- exceptionally(Function<Throwable, T>): Recovers from an exception by providing a fallback default.
- handle(BiFunction<T, Throwable, U>): Inspects both success result and exception, transforming either into a final output.

topics.shortDescription: High-concurrency data structures: ConcurrentHashMap (CAS and bucket locks), CopyOnWriteArrayList, BlockingQueue (Producer-Consumer pattern), and atomic compound operations.
learningObjectives: Explain why synchronized collection wrappers (Collections.synchronizedMap) cause bottleneck contention under high concurrency
Deconstruct ConcurrentHashMap internal mechanics: lock-free reads, CAS bucket updates, and synchronized bin heads
Understand CopyOnWriteArrayList: immutable snapshots, copy-on-mutation trade-offs, and read-heavy use cases

topics.conceptExplanation:
Standard Java collections (HashMap, ArrayList) are not thread-safe. Wrapping them with Collections.synchronizedMap() or Collections.synchronizedList() introduces a single global mutex lock on the entire collection, degrading multi-threaded throughput. The java.util.concurrent package provides lock-optimized, high-concurrency collections.

1. ConcurrentHashMap Internals:
- Reads (get, containsKey) are completely lock-free and never block, reading volatile node fields directly.
- Writes (put, remove) do NOT lock the entire map. If a bucket is empty, it inserts the node using a lock-free Compare-And-Swap (CAS). If a collision occurs, it synchronizes ONLY on the head node of that specific bucket (bin lock), allowing concurrent writes to all other buckets.
- ConcurrentHashMap disallows null keys and null values.

2. CopyOnWriteArrayList:
- Every mutating operation (add, set, remove) creates an entirely new underlying copy of the backing array.
- Iterators operate on an immutable snapshot taken at iterator creation time; they never throw ConcurrentModificationException.
- Ideal for read-heavy, write-rare workloads (e.g., event listener lists, observer registries).

3. BlockingQueue & Producer-Consumer:
- BlockingQueue provides blocking operations: put(e) blocks if queue is full; take() blocks if queue is empty.
- Implementations include ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded circular array) and LinkedBlockingQueue (optionally bounded).
- Forms the foundation of thread-safe Producer-Consumer pipelines.

topics.shortDescription: Deconstruct the JVM runtime architecture: Heap generations (Eden, Survivor, Tenured), Metaspace, GC roots and reachability, reference types (Strong, Soft, Weak, Phantom), and memory leaks.
learningObjectives: Deconstruct JVM runtime data areas: Heap, Thread Call Stack, Metaspace, and Program Counter registers

topics.conceptExplanation:
To build high-performance, fault-tolerant Java systems, developers must understand how the JVM manages memory and reclaims unreferenced objects.

1. JVM Memory Areas:
- Heap Memory: Shared across all threads. Stores all instantiated objects and their instance variables.
- Thread Call Stack: Private to each thread. Stores local primitive variables, method execution frames, and references to heap objects.
- Metaspace: Replaced PermGen in Java 8. Stored in native OS memory; holds loaded class metadata, bytecode, and static variables.

2. Generational Garbage Collection Hypothesis:
Empirical analysis reveals that the vast majority of Java objects die shortly after creation. The heap is divided into:
- Young Generation:
  * Eden Space: Newly allocated objects land here.
  * Survivor Spaces (S0 and S1): Objects surviving a Minor GC are copied back and forth between S0 and S1.
- Old / Tenured Generation: Objects that survive multiple GC cycles (reaching the age threshold, typically 15) are promoted here. Reclaimed during Major / Full GC (costlier Stop-The-World pause).

3. Reachability & GC Roots:
The garbage collector traces objects starting from GC Roots (active stack frame references, static variables, active JNI pointers). An object is eligible for garbage collection if it is unreachable from any GC root.

4. Java Reference Types (java.lang.ref):
- Strong Reference (default): new Object(). Never collected while referenced.
- SoftReference<T>: Collected only before OutOfMemoryError occurs; ideal for memory-sensitive caches.
- WeakReference<T>: Collected immediately during the next GC cycle if no strong references exist; powers WeakHashMap.
- PhantomReference<T>: Enqueued after finalization; used for pre-mortem cleanup without reviving objects.

5. Common Memory Leaks: Static collections accumulating items indefinitely, unremoved listeners/callbacks, unclosed database/file streams, and improper equals/hashCode leading to orphaned Map entries.

topics.shortDescription: High-throughput Java engineering: algorithmic complexity, StringBuilder vs string concatenation, autoboxing overhead, stream vs loop benchmarks, and JMH micro-benchmarking.
learningObjectives: Evaluate time and space complexity trade-offs across Java collections and algorithms

topics.conceptExplanation:
Writing high-performance Java code requires balancing algorithmic complexity, memory allocation rates, and CPU cache efficiency.

1. String Concatenation vs StringBuilder:
In Java, String is immutable. Writing str += item inside a loop of N iterations creates N new StringBuilder and String objects, copying characters repeatedly in quadratic O(N^2) time. Using a single pre-sized StringBuilder converts this to linear O(N) time.

2. The Hidden Cost of Autoboxing:
Autoboxing (e.g., converting primitive int to Integer) allocates an object wrapper on the heap. In tight loops or large collections, accumulating with Long sum = 0L; sum += i; creates millions of ephemeral Long objects, causing severe Garbage Collection pressure. Always prefer primitive types (long, int) and primitive collections (LongConsumer, IntStream, IntBuffer) in performance-critical paths.

3. Streams vs Imperative Loops:
- For small collections (< 100 elements), traditional indexed or enhanced for-loops are often faster because they avoid stream pipeline object creation and lambda allocation.
- For large datasets, complex transformations, or parallel workloads, Streams provide superior readability, maintainability, and clean parallelization.

4. Presizing Collections:
Always pass expected sizes to collection constructors: new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) or new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75f + 1). This eliminates costly backing array reallocations and rehashing.

5. Micro-Benchmarking with JMH:
Never benchmark Java code using simple System.currentTimeMillis() loops. JIT compiler warm-up, dead code elimination, and loop unrolling produce misleading results. Always use the Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH).

learningObjectives: Architect a multi-threaded task management system combining all advanced Java concepts learned across the track

topics.conceptExplanation:
This capstone mini project integrates the complete set of concepts mastered throughout this course:

1. Domain Modeling with Records and Enums:
- TaskPriority enum (CRITICAL(1), HIGH(2), MEDIUM(3), LOW(4))
- Immutable Task record with fields: id, title, category, priority, estimatedDurationMs, and status

2. Specialized Collections Architecture:
- PriorityQueue<Task>: Schedules tasks ordered by priority severity.
- ConcurrentHashMap<String, Task>: Provides thread-safe O(1) state lookups for running and completed tasks.
- Map<String, List<Task>>: Categorizes tasks by department/category via Stream groupingBy.

3. Concurrency & Asynchronous Pipelines:
- ExecutorService with fixed worker threads executing tasks in parallel.
- CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() to dispatch tasks asynchronously and attach callbacks for progress tracking.
- AtomicInteger counters for thread-safe completed task tracking.

4. Robust Error Handling & File Persistence:
- Custom InvalidTaskException validating task invariants.
- Java NIO.2 Files and try-with-resources exporting summary reports to disk.

5. Generics & Functional Utilities:
- Generic task filter and aggregator utilities applying Predicate<Task> and Function<Task, R>.
